option_description: Controls whether DNSSEC signing is active for a DNS zone, resulting in cryptographic RRSIG records being generated for all zone records and a DNSKEY record being published at the zone apex. This is the foundational signing toggle that must be enabled before any DNSSEC validation chain can be established.
security_impact: Referenced by origin_authenticity_verification, negative_response_authentication, zone_signing_completeness, and signature_expiry_monitoring rules. The Rego policy requires dnssec_enabled == true as a prerequisite for origin authenticity (with ds_record_published and enforced validation mode), negative response authentication (with NSEC/NSEC3 proof type), zone signing completeness (with 100% RRSIG coverage), and signature expiry monitoring. Without this enabled, no downstream DNSSEC protections can activate.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the zone's SOA record with DNSSEC DO bit set to check for RRSIG records accompanying the response.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response includes an RRSIG record alongside the SOA record. If only SOA is returned without RRSIG, DNSSEC signing is not enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the DNSKEY record type at the zone apex to confirm a public key is published.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more DNSKEY records returned (e.g., '257 3 13 <base64-key>'). Empty response indicates DNSSEC is not enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log into the DNS provider or registrar management console (e.g., Route 53, Cloudflare, GoDaddy) and navigate to the DNS zone settings for the domain to check DNSSEC signing status.
how_to_obtain.navigation: DNS Provider Console → DNS Management → Select Zone → DNSSEC or Zone Signing Settings → Check 'Enabled' / 'Active' status indicator
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A status indicator showing DNSSEC is 'Enabled', 'Active', or 'Signed', along with key tag and algorithm details.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use an online DNSSEC analysis tool to verify signing status and visualize the signing configuration.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Alternatively browse to https://dnsviz.net/d/example.com/analyze/ or https://dnssec-debugger.verisignlabs.com/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Google DNS JSON response shows 'Answer' array with DNSKEY records and 'AD' (Authenticated Data) flag set to true.

option_description: Confirms that DNSSEC signing is operationally active on the authoritative nameserver for the zone, verified by querying the authoritative server directly for DNSKEY and RRSIG records at the zone apex. This distinguishes between signing being configured in a control panel versus being actively served by the authoritative nameserver.
security_impact: Referenced exclusively by the chain_of_trust_coverage rule. The Rego policy requires dnssec_enabled_at_zone == true alongside ds_record_published_at_parent == true and root_to_tld_trust_anchor_validated == true to establish full Chain of Trust Coverage. If the authoritative server is not actively serving signed records, the chain of trust cannot be validated even if signing was configured at the registrar level.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the authoritative nameserver directly for DNSKEY records to confirm signing is active at the source, bypassing caching resolvers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DNSKEY records are returned in the ANSWER section. An RRSIG record covering the DNSKEY RRset should also be present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the authoritative nameservers first, then query each one for RRSIG records at the SOA to confirm signing is active on all authoritative servers.
how_to_obtain.command: NS=$(dig +short NS example.com | head -1); dig SOA example.com @$NS +dnssec | grep -E 'RRSIG|DNSKEY|SOA'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output contains RRSIG records in the ANSWER section alongside the SOA record, confirming the authoritative server is actively signing.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use delv (DNSSEC-aware dig) to perform full validation against the authoritative zone and confirm signing is active.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows 'fully validated' or lists RRSIG inception/expiration timestamps, confirming active zone signing.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use DNSViz to perform an authoritative-aware analysis that distinguishes between what is configured and what is actually being served by authoritative nameservers.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Browse to https://dnsviz.net/d/example.com/analyze/ and review the 'Authoritative' section for DNSKEY and RRSIG presence on each listed nameserver.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All authoritative nameservers shown as serving DNSKEY and RRSIG records with no delegation errors at the zone apex level.

option_description: Tracks whether a Delegation Signer (DS) record has been submitted to and published by the parent zone (typically the TLD registry), which cryptographically links the parent zone's trust to the child zone's Key Signing Key (KSK). Without this record, even a fully signed zone cannot be validated through the standard chain of trust.
security_impact: Referenced by origin_authenticity_verification, negative_response_authentication, and zone_signing_completeness rules. The Rego policy requires ds_record_published == true in combination with dnssec_enabled == true for origin authenticity (proving responses genuinely originate from the authoritative zone owner) and negative response authentication (authenticating NXDOMAIN/NODATA responses). Zone signing completeness also requires it alongside 100% RRSIG coverage. Without the DS record, all signing effort in the child zone is unverifiable by standard resolvers.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the parent TLD nameserver directly for DS records for the target domain to confirm the registry has published the delegation signer.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more DS records returned (e.g., '12345 13 2 <hex-digest>'). Empty response means the DS record has not been submitted to or published by the registry.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query any recursive resolver for the DS record and verify the AD flag is set, confirming both publication and validation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DS record returned in ANSWER section with the 'ad' flag set in the response header flags line.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the registrar's DNSSEC management interface to confirm the DS record has been submitted to the registry.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Registrar Account → Domain Management → Select Domain → DNSSEC Settings or DS Records → View published DS record(s) with key tag, algorithm, and digest type
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one DS record entry showing key tag, algorithm number, digest type (2 = SHA-256 recommended), and digest value matching the zone's KSK.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the DNSSEC Debugger to visualize DS record publication and validate the hash matches the child zone's KSK.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Alternatively use https://dnssec-debugger.verisignlabs.com/ and enter the domain name to see DS record status at the parent zone.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DS record present in JSON 'Answer' array. The key tag value should match the key tag of the KSK DNSKEY record in the child zone.

option_description: Specifically verifies that the DS record for the zone is published in the TLD (parent) zone, establishing the delegation trust link that connects the zone signing keys to the parent zone's chain of trust. This attribute is evaluated from the parent zone's perspective and is essential for end-to-end DNSSEC validation paths.
security_impact: Referenced exclusively by the chain_of_trust_coverage rule alongside dnssec_enabled_at_zone and root_to_tld_trust_anchor_validated. The Rego policy requires all three to be true to establish Chain of Trust Coverage, which provides end-to-end trust continuity from root through TLD to the authoritative zone. A missing DS record at the parent means the zone's signing is cryptographically isolated and resolvers performing DNSSEC validation will treat the zone as unsigned or bogus.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the TLD nameserver directly for the DS record of the target zone to confirm the parent-level delegation signer is published.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ANSWER section contains one or more DS records with key tag, algorithm, digest type, and digest fields. AUTHORITY section without DS records indicates the DS is not published.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify the correct parent nameserver for less common TLDs and query it specifically for the DS record.
how_to_obtain.command: PARENT_NS=$(dig +short NS com. | head -1); dig DS example.com @$PARENT_NS
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DS record in ANSWER section. If NOERROR with empty ANSWER and NSEC/NSEC3 in AUTHORITY, the DS is definitively absent at the parent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the whois lookup to identify the registrar and then verify the DS record was properly transmitted from registrar to registry.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: WHOIS output shows 'DNSSEC: signedDelegation' or lists DS record data. 'DNSSEC: unsigned' indicates the DS record has not been submitted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use DNSViz analysis to see the parent-to-child delegation link visualization and confirm DS record publication at the TLD level.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Navigate to https://dnsviz.net/d/example.com/analyze/ and examine the graphical chain of trust, specifically the DS record arrow between the TLD zone and the domain zone.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DNSViz shows a solid arrow (not dashed) between the TLD zone and the child zone representing the DS delegation, with no error icons on the DS record node.

option_description: Verifies that the TLD itself participates in the global DNSSEC chain of trust by having a DS record published in the ICANN root zone, confirming that the trust chain extends from the root trust anchor (managed by IANA) through the TLD down to the domain zone. This is typically true for major TLDs but must be verified for less common or ccTLDs.
security_impact: Referenced exclusively by chain_of_trust_coverage rule. The Rego policy requires root_to_tld_trust_anchor_validated == true as the topmost link in the chain of trust hierarchy. Without this, the entire downstream DNSSEC validation for domains under that TLD is unanchored from the global root trust. This particularly matters for ccTLDs and newer gTLDs that may not have joined the signed root zone, making chain-of-trust-based validations impossible regardless of zone-level DNSSEC configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query a root nameserver directly for the DS record of the TLD to confirm root-to-TLD trust anchor publication.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more DS records returned for the TLD (e.g., '30909 8 2 <digest>'). Empty response means the TLD does not have a DS record in the root zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check multiple root servers for consistency and retrieve the full DS record details for verification.
how_to_obtain.command: for root in a b c d e; do echo "--- ${root}.root-servers.net ---"; dig DS com. @${root}.root-servers.net +short; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All root servers return identical DS record(s) for the TLD. Consistent results across root servers confirm stable root-to-TLD trust anchor publication.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use IANA's root zone database or query the signed root zone data to verify TLD signing status.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DNSKEY and RRSIG records returned for the TLD zone apex, confirming the TLD is signed. Cross-reference with IANA root zone file at https://www.iana.org/domains/root/files.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the ICANN DNSSEC root zone portal or DNSSEC analyzer to verify TLD signing status from authoritative IANA sources.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Browse to https://stats.research.icann.org/dns/tld_report/ and check TLD signing status, or use https://dnsviz.net/d/com./analyze/ to view the root-to-TLD delegation chain.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TLD listed as 'Signed' in ICANN TLD report, or DNSViz shows a valid DS record arrow from the root zone to the TLD zone with no validation errors.

option_description: Controls whether the DNS resolver software actively performs cryptographic validation of DNSSEC signatures on DNS responses it receives. When enabled, the resolver checks RRSIG records against DNSKEY records and follows the chain of trust to the configured trust anchor before returning results to clients.
security_impact: Referenced by response_integrity_validation, validation_failure_detection, and resolver_validation_enforcement rules. The Rego policy requires dnssec_validation_enabled == true as a prerequisite for all three resolver-side protections. Without this, the resolver accepts DNS responses without any cryptographic verification, making it susceptible to cache poisoning and DNS spoofing attacks. It must be combined with trust_anchor_configured and dnssec_validation_mode == 'enforce' for full Response Integrity Validation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the BIND named.conf configuration file for the dnssec-validation directive in the options block.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Line containing 'dnssec-validation yes;' or 'dnssec-validation auto;' indicates validation is enabled. 'dnssec-validation no;' or absence of the directive means validation is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Unbound resolver configuration for DNSSEC validation modules and settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: module-config includes 'validator' (e.g., 'module-config: "validator iterator"') and auto-trust-anchor-file is set, confirming validation is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check PowerDNS Recursor configuration for DNSSEC validation mode setting.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Line containing 'dnssec=validate' or 'dnssec=process' indicates validation is active. 'dnssec=off' or absent means disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test the resolver's validation behavior by querying a known DNSSEC-invalid domain and checking for SERVFAIL response.
how_to_obtain.command: dig @127.0.0.1 dnssec-failed.org A && echo 'VALIDATION NOT ENFORCED' || echo 'VALIDATION ENFORCED - SERVFAIL received'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A SERVFAIL response (exit code non-zero with 'status: SERVFAIL') from querying dnssec-failed.org confirms DNSSEC validation is enabled. A successful A record response means validation is not enforced.

option_description: Controls whether the DNS resolver has a valid DNSSEC trust anchor configured, which serves as the cryptographic root of trust for validating the entire DNSSEC chain. The trust anchor is typically the ICANN root zone KSK (Key Signing Key), from which all zone-level signature validations are derived hierarchically.
security_impact: Referenced by response_integrity_validation, validation_failure_detection, and resolver_validation_enforcement rules. The Rego policy requires trust_anchor_configured == true alongside dnssec_validation_enabled for all three countermeasures. Without a trust anchor, the resolver has no cryptographic reference point from which to validate the chain of trust, meaning DNSSEC validation is either non-functional or relies on an unverified starting point. An outdated trust anchor (e.g., after a KSK rollover) will cause all DNSSEC validation to fail.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check BIND for trust anchor configuration in named.conf, looking for managed-keys, trust-anchors, or root.key file inclusion.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of 'trust-anchors { . initial-key 257 3 8 "<base64-KSK>"; };' or 'managed-keys' block, or an included root.key file containing the current IANA KSK (key tag 20326 as of 2017 KSK rollover).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Unbound for auto-trust-anchor-file configuration which manages the root trust anchor automatically.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration shows 'auto-trust-anchor-file: /var/lib/unbound/root.key' and the root.key file contains a DNSKEY record for the root zone with the current KSK key tag.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the configured trust anchor key tag matches the current IANA root KSK by comparing against the published root anchors XML.
how_to_obtain.command: dig DNSKEY . @a.root-servers.net +short | awk '{print $4}' | base64 -d | sha256sum; curl -s https://data.iana.org/root-anchors/root-anchors.xml | grep -o 'KeyTag>[0-9]*</KeyTag'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The key tag from the local trust anchor file matches one of the KeyTag values in the IANA root-anchors.xml (currently 20326). A mismatch indicates an outdated or incorrect trust anchor.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use systemd-resolved DNSSEC configuration check for systems using systemd as the DNS resolver.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: resolved.conf shows 'DNSSEC=yes' and resolvectl status shows 'DNSSEC setting: yes' and 'DNSSEC supported: yes' with a listed trust anchor.

option_description: Specifies the enforcement strictness of DNSSEC validation at the resolver level, with three distinct behavioral modes: 'enforce' causes the resolver to return SERVFAIL for unsigned or invalid DNSSEC responses (hard-fail), 'permissive' logs validation failures but returns the response anyway (soft-fail/advisory), and 'disabled' performs no DNSSEC validation regardless of other settings.
security_impact: Referenced by response_integrity_validation and origin_authenticity_verification rules. The Rego policy requires dnssec_validation_mode == 'enforce' for Response Integrity Validation (combined with dnssec_validation_enabled and trust_anchor_configured) and dnssec_validation_mode == 'enforced' for Origin Authenticity Verification (combined with dnssec_enabled and ds_record_published). Only enforce mode provides actual security guarantees - permissive mode may log attacks but does not prevent clients from receiving tampered DNS responses. Disabled mode provides no protection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check BIND named.conf for the dnssec-validation directive value, which maps to enforce (yes/auto) or disabled (no).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'dnssec-validation yes;' = enforce mode, 'dnssec-validation auto;' = enforce with auto-managed keys, 'dnssec-validation no;' = disabled mode. BIND has no native permissive mode; permissive behavior requires custom RPZ or logging configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check PowerDNS Recursor configuration for the dnssec setting which maps directly to validation modes.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'dnssec=validate' = enforce mode, 'dnssec=process' or 'dnssec=process-no-validate' = permissive mode, 'dnssec=off' or 'dnssec=no' = disabled. 'dnssec=log-fail' = permissive with logging.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Behaviorally test the resolver's validation mode by querying a deliberately broken DNSSEC domain and a known-good signed domain.
how_to_obtain.command: echo 'Testing enforce mode:'; dig @127.0.0.1 dnssec-failed.org A +short; echo 'Exit code:' $?; echo 'Testing permissive (should succeed):'; dig @127.0.0.1 cloudflare.com A +short | head -2
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Enforce mode: dnssec-failed.org returns SERVFAIL (empty output, exit code 9 or 10). Permissive mode: dnssec-failed.org returns an A record despite invalid DNSSEC. cloudflare.com should return an IP in both modes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Unbound configuration for DNSSEC validation strictness settings including val-permissive-mode.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'val-permissive-mode: no' with validator in module-config = enforce mode. 'val-permissive-mode: yes' = permissive mode. Absence of 'validator' in module-config = disabled mode.

option_description: Controls the action taken by the resolver when DNSSEC signature validation fails or signatures are missing for signed zones. Options are 'block' (return SERVFAIL to clients), 'log_only' (log failures but forward responses), or 'permissive' (no enforcement).
security_impact: This attribute is a direct input to the validation_failure_detection Rego rule, which only fires when validation_failure_action == 'block'. Without blocking, forged or tampered DNS responses can be forwarded to clients even when DNSSEC validation detects a mismatch. A 'permissive' or 'log_only' setting renders DNSSEC validation operationally inert from a protection standpoint, allowing cache poisoning attacks to succeed silently.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the BIND named.conf for the dnssec-validation directive. The value 'yes' enforces blocking (SERVFAIL on failure); 'no' disables enforcement entirely; 'auto' enables with managed trust anchors but may differ in strictness.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: dnssec-validation yes; indicates blocking mode is active

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Unbound resolvers, inspect the unbound.conf for the val-permissive-mode directive. 'no' means bogus responses are blocked; 'yes' means log_only behavior.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: val-permissive-mode: no indicates blocking enforcement

how_to_obtain.instruction: For PowerDNS Recursor, query the running configuration via the rec_control tool to check the active dnssec setting.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: dnssec=validate indicates hard blocking; dnssec=process-no-validate indicates permissive

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query a known DNSSEC-bogus test domain against the resolver to observe whether it returns SERVFAIL (block) or an answer (permissive/log_only).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: status: SERVFAIL confirms blocking mode is active

option_description: Defines how the resolver handles DNS queries that arrive with the CD (Checking Disabled) bit set in the query header. 'hard_fail' enforces DNSSEC validation regardless of the CD flag; 'permissive' allows the CD flag to bypass validation; 'off' means validation is not performed at all.
security_impact: The resolver_validation_enforcement Rego rule fires for cd_flag_enforcement_mode == 'hard_fail' as the strongest enforcement path, and also accepts 'permissive' only when paired with reject_bogus_only unsigned zone acceptance. If set to 'permissive' or 'off', any client or attacker that sets the CD bit on a query can trivially bypass DNSSEC validation, nullifying the protection DNSSEC provides. This is a common bypass vector in environments with stub resolvers or misconfigured forwarders.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In BIND, check whether dnssec-validation is 'yes' (hard_fail — CD flag is overridden) versus 'auto' or 'no'. BIND with 'yes' ignores the CD flag from clients.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: dnssec-validation yes; maps to hard_fail behavior

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Unbound, the 'ignore-cd: no' directive (default) means the resolver respects the CD flag from clients (permissive). Setting 'ignore-cd: yes' forces validation regardless of the CD flag (hard_fail).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ignore-cd: yes indicates hard_fail enforcement

how_to_obtain.instruction: In PowerDNS Recursor, check the recursor.conf for the dnssec directive. 'dnssec=validate' enforces validation (hard_fail); 'dnssec=process' respects CD flags (permissive).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: dnssec=validate confirms hard_fail mode

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send a query with the CD bit set to a known bogus domain and observe whether the resolver validates anyway. A SERVFAIL despite CD set indicates hard_fail.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SERVFAIL returned even with +cd flag confirms hard_fail enforcement

option_description: Governs resolver behavior when processing responses from zones that have not been signed with DNSSEC. 'reject_bogus_only' passes unsigned zones but blocks forged signatures; 'accept_all_unsigned' applies no distinction; 'reject_unsigned' requires all zones to be signed.
security_impact: This attribute is evaluated in the resolver_validation_enforcement Rego rule as a secondary condition — when cd_flag_enforcement_mode is 'permissive', unsigned_zone_acceptance must be 'reject_bogus_only' for the countermeasure to apply. Setting this to 'accept_all_unsigned' effectively disables meaningful DNSSEC enforcement because resolvers will process all unauthenticated responses without distinction, making DNS cache poisoning trivial for unsigned zones. The default 'accept_all_unsigned' is the most common insecure configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In BIND, 'dnssec-validation yes' enables reject_bogus_only behavior — unsigned zones resolve but bogus (signature-failed) responses are blocked. If dnssec-validation is 'no', this maps to accept_all_unsigned.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: dnssec-validation yes; maps to reject_bogus_only

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Unbound, check 'val-permissive-mode' — if 'no', unsigned zones pass (reject_bogus_only) but bogus signatures fail. Also check 'harden-dnssec-stripped' which controls whether stripped DNSSEC is treated as bogus.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: val-permissive-mode: no and harden-dnssec-stripped: yes indicates reject_bogus_only

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query a domain in a signed zone that has intentionally bad signatures to confirm the resolver rejects bogus data, then query an unsigned zone to confirm it still resolves.
how_to_obtain.command: dig @<resolver-ip> dnssec-failed.org A; dig @<resolver-ip> example.com A
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SERVFAIL for dnssec-failed.org and NOERROR for example.com confirms reject_bogus_only

how_to_obtain.instruction: In cloud-managed DNS resolvers (e.g., AWS Route53 Resolver, Cloudflare Gateway), navigate to DNS Firewall or Resolver security settings and review the DNSSEC validation policy toggle to determine the enforcement level.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > Route53 > Resolver > Security policies > DNSSEC validation
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DNSSEC validation enabled with enforcement mode displayed

option_description: Specifies the mechanism used to cryptographically authenticate NXDOMAIN and NODATA (negative) DNS responses. NSEC provides authenticated denial of existence with ordered record chains; NSEC3 provides hashed denial to prevent zone enumeration; 'none' means negative responses are unauthenticated.
security_impact: This attribute is a direct input to the negative_response_authentication Rego rule, which requires negative_response_proof_type to be either 'nsec' or 'nsec3' (combined with dnssec_enabled and ds_record_published) to activate the countermeasure. Without authenticated negative responses, an attacker can inject false NXDOMAIN replies to redirect users, cause denial of service, or suppress DNS-based security lookups. NSEC3 is preferred over NSEC in public-facing zones because NSEC allows zone walking (full zone enumeration), which exposes all hostnames.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query a non-existent name in the target zone and inspect the authority section of the response for NSEC or NSEC3 records.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Authority section containing NSEC or NSEC3 records with valid RRSIG signatures

how_to_obtain.instruction: In BIND with dnssec-policy configured, check the policy block in named.conf for the 'nsec3param' directive to confirm NSEC3 is in use, or its absence indicating NSEC.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: nsec3param 1 0 10 <salt>; confirms NSEC3 is configured

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use ldns-walk or dnssec-walk tools to attempt NSEC zone walking against the zone. Successful enumeration confirms NSEC; failure or hashed names confirms NSEC3.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Hashed labels returned confirm NSEC3; cleartext labels confirm NSEC

how_to_obtain.instruction: In cloud DNS providers such as AWS Route53 or Cloudflare, navigate to the DNSSEC configuration panel for the hosted zone to view the configured denial-of-existence type.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > Route53 > Hosted Zones > <zone> > DNSSEC signing > View DNSSEC details
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NSEC3 displayed as the denial-of-existence type in zone settings

option_description: Represents the percentage of DNS resource record sets (RRsets) within a zone that have valid, non-expired RRSIG signatures actively covering them. A value of 100 means all RRsets are signed; lower values indicate gaps in signing coverage.
security_impact: The zone_signing_completeness Rego rule requires rrsig_coverage_percentage >= 100 to activate the countermeasure. Any RRset without a valid RRSIG is effectively unauthenticated even in a DNSSEC-enabled zone — an attacker can spoof responses for unsigned record types (e.g., MX, TXT, SPF) without triggering validation failures. Partial coverage creates exploitable blind spots that undermine the integrity guarantees DNSSEC is intended to provide across the full zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a zone transfer (AXFR) and count total RRsets versus RRsets with accompanying RRSIG records to calculate coverage percentage.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Coverage: 100% indicates full RRSIG coverage across all RRsets

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the 'dnssec-verify' tool on a zone file export to identify any unsigned or incorrectly signed RRsets within the zone.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: zone fully signed confirms 100% coverage; error messages identify unsigned RRsets

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the 'zonemaster-cli' or 'drill' to probe specific record types for RRSIG presence across expected RRsets (SOA, NS, MX, A, AAAA, TXT).
how_to_obtain.command: for rtype in SOA NS MX A AAAA TXT; do drill -D <zone> $rtype @<authoritative-ns> | grep -E 'RRSIG|$rtype'; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RRSIG records present alongside each queried record type

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cloud-managed zones (e.g., AWS Route53), use the AWS CLI to list resource record sets and verify RRSIG records are present for each resource type.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RRSIG entries listed for each corresponding record type in the zone

option_description: Indicates whether automated monitoring or alerting systems are configured to detect RRSIG records approaching or past their expiration timestamp before signatures lapse and cause validation failures.
security_impact: The signature_expiry_monitoring Rego rule requires signature_expiry_monitoring_enabled == true (combined with alert_threshold_days_before_expiry >= 1) to activate the countermeasure. Expired RRSIG records cause DNSSEC-validating resolvers to return SERVFAIL for the entire zone, creating a complete DNS outage for all clients using validating resolvers. Without proactive monitoring, expired signatures may go undetected until users report failures, potentially causing extended outages. Many high-profile DNSSEC failures have resulted from unmonitored signature expiration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the DNS operations team or review runbooks to determine whether RRSIG expiry monitoring jobs exist. Ask for evidence of configured monitoring tools such as Nagios, Zabbix, Datadog, or Prometheus DNS exporters.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented monitoring job or ticket referencing RRSIG expiry checks with configured alerting

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search for scheduled cron jobs or systemd timers that run RRSIG expiry checks using dig, check_dns, or custom scripts.
how_to_obtain.command: crontab -l 2>/dev/null; systemctl list-timers | grep -i dns; find /etc/cron* /var/spool/cron -type f 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -l 'rrsig\|dnssec\|expir' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Cron entries or systemd timers referencing RRSIG or DNSSEC expiry checking scripts

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check monitoring platforms (Nagios, Zabbix, Datadog, PagerDuty) for DNS/DNSSEC check definitions. In Nagios, look for check_dns or check_rrsig service definitions; in Datadog, look for DNS synthetic tests with DNSSEC validation.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Nagios > Services > Filter by 'DNSSEC' or 'RRSIG'; Datadog > Synthetics > DNS Tests > Filter by zone
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active monitoring check for RRSIG expiry with notification contacts configured

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review SIEM or monitoring system logs for DNS-related alert history to confirm that RRSIG expiry alerts have fired historically, indicating the monitoring system is operational.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing historical RRSIG expiry alert events

option_description: Specifies the number of days before an RRSIG record expires at which monitoring systems should trigger an alert. A value of zero indicates no advance warning is configured, meaning alerts only fire after expiration has already occurred.
security_impact: The signature_expiry_monitoring Rego rule requires alert_threshold_days_before_expiry >= 1 (paired with signature_expiry_monitoring_enabled == true) to activate the countermeasure. Insufficient lead time is operationally dangerous — key rollover and re-signing operations require time to propagate through the DNS hierarchy and be cached by resolvers. Industry best practice recommends 7–14 days of advance notice to allow operators time to respond before outages occur. A threshold of 0 means monitoring is reactive rather than preventive, defeating the purpose of proactive alerting.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Nagios or Icinga service check definitions for RRSIG expiry checks to identify the configured warning threshold value.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: check_rrsig -w 14 -c 7 showing 14-day warning and 7-day critical thresholds

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Zabbix, query the database or use the API to retrieve trigger configurations for DNS/DNSSEC-related items to identify the configured threshold days.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Trigger expression showing threshold days in the condition (e.g., last()}<14)

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Datadog Synthetics or PagerDuty, review the DNS test or alert rule settings for the zone to identify the configured days-before-expiry threshold for DNSSEC signature alerts.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Datadog > Synthetics > DNS Tests > <test> > Alert Conditions > DNSSEC threshold setting
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Alert threshold showing value between 7-14 days before expiry

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review documentation or interview the DNS operations team to confirm the organization's defined SLA for RRSIG expiry alerting lead time and verify this matches the monitoring configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented policy specifying minimum alert threshold (e.g., 14 days) matching the monitoring configuration

option_description: Indicates whether formal, scheduled procedures for rotating both the Key Signing Key (KSK) and Zone Signing Key (ZSK) are documented and actively configured within the DNSSEC management system, covering both automated and manually scheduled rollover workflows.
security_impact: The key_rollover_operational_continuity Rego rule requires key_rollover_procedure_configured == true as the primary condition (combined with pre_publish_overlap_enabled and rollover_automation_status) to activate the countermeasure. Without configured rollover procedures, DNSSEC keys remain in use indefinitely, increasing cryptographic exposure risk over time. Additionally, ad-hoc emergency rollovers performed without defined procedures frequently cause outages due to missed DS record publication steps or inadequate TTL waiting periods. Proper rollover configuration using pre-publish methodology ensures continuous validation coverage without resolver failures.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In BIND 9.16+ with KASP (Key and Signing Policy Automation), inspect named.conf for dnssec-policy blocks that define KSK and ZSK lifetimes and rollover parameters.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy block showing keys { ksk lifetime <period>; zsk lifetime <period>; } confirming rollover is scheduled

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for OpenDNSSEC configuration files that define kasp.xml policies, which govern automated KSK and ZSK rollover schedules.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: KSK and ZSK Lifetime elements present with defined rollover periods (e.g., P1Y for KSK, P90D for ZSK)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search for cron jobs, systemd timers, or automation scripts that perform DNSSEC key rollovers using tools like dnssec-rollerd, ods-enforcer, or custom scripts.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Cron or systemd service files referencing key rollover automation scripts

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request and review the organization's DNSSEC key management policy documentation, change management records, or runbooks to confirm that KSK and ZSK rollover procedures are formally defined with scheduled intervals and responsible owners.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented procedure specifying KSK rollover interval (typically 1-2 years), ZSK rollover interval (typically 30-90 days), responsible team, and step-by-step DS record publication process

option_description: Controls whether new DNSSEC keys are published into the zone before old keys are retired, creating an overlap window during key rollovers that ensures validators holding cached old keys can still verify signatures until the cache TTL expires and they fetch the new key.
security_impact: Directly governs key_rollover_operational_continuity in the Rego policy. The rule requires pre_publish_overlap_enabled == true alongside key_rollover_procedure_configured == true to fire, meaning without overlap enabled the countermeasure is not credited. Without pre-publication, validators caching the old DNSKEY may receive responses signed only with the new key, causing SERVFAIL errors and potential denial of service during the rollover window.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the BIND KASP (Key and Signing Policy) configuration to verify the rollover method is set to pre-publish or double-ksk. In BIND 9.16+ named.conf or a dnssec-policy block, look for the 'roll-method' directive or the presence of both 'publish' and 'activate' timing offsets.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A dnssec-policy block such as: 'keys { ksk key-directory lifetime unlimited algorithm ecdsap256sha256; zsk key-directory lifetime P90D algorithm ecdsap256sha256; };' with publish-safety and retire-safety intervals defined, indicating overlap is accommodated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all DNSKEY records for the zone and compare timestamps to determine whether new keys are published before old ones are retired. Look for two active KSK or ZSK entries simultaneously, indicating an overlap period.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Two DNSKEY records with the same algorithm but different key tags present simultaneously during rollover, confirming pre-publication overlap is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For OpenDNSSEC deployments, inspect the KASP XML policy file to confirm the PropagationDelay and SafetyMargin values create sufficient overlap between key publication and retirement.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: PublishSafety and RetireSafety elements with positive durations (e.g., PT3600S) confirming overlap windows are defined in the signing policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview DNS administrators or review runbooks to determine whether the key rollover procedure document explicitly includes a pre-publication step, TTL wait period, and confirmation check before retiring the old key.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented rollover procedure with explicit steps: (1) publish new key, (2) wait for max zone TTL, (3) begin signing with new key, (4) wait for max RRSIG TTL, (5) retire old key.

option_description: Describes whether DNSSEC key signing key (KSK) and zone signing key (ZSK) rollovers are handled by automated tooling without manual intervention, are scheduled manually by operators on a calendar-driven basis, or have no rollover process configured at all.
security_impact: Used alongside pre_publish_overlap_enabled in the key_rollover_operational_continuity Rego rule. Both 'automated' and 'manual_scheduled' values satisfy the rule when combined with pre_publish_overlap_enabled == true, but 'not_configured' will never satisfy it. Automated rollover eliminates the risk of key expiry due to operator oversight, while manual_scheduled introduces dependency on human scheduling reliability. Keys that never roll over increase exposure window if private key material is compromised.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For BIND 9.16+ with inline signing and KASP, check named.conf for 'dnssec-policy' directive assignments on zone blocks. Presence of a named or built-in policy with lifetime values indicates automated rollover is configured.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zone stanzas containing 'dnssec-policy default;' or a named custom policy, indicating BIND's automatic key management is active. Absence of dnssec-policy with manual key files suggests manual_scheduled or not_configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For BIND, list managed DNSSEC keys in the key directory and inspect their timing metadata to determine if BIND is autonomously scheduling rollovers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Timestamps set for future Retire and Delete events indicate automated scheduling. Only Publish and Activate dates with no Retire/Delete indicates manual process.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS Route 53 DNSSEC, use the AWS CLI to inspect the DNSSEC signing configuration and check whether key management is delegated to Route 53 automation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output of 'SIGNING' confirms Route 53 is managing signatures automatically. Check KeySigningKeys array for Status='ACTIVE' with AWS-managed keys indicating full automation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the DNS change management calendar, ticketing system, or cron job schedules to determine if key rollovers are triggered by an automated scheduler or require manual operator initiation.
how_to_obtain.command: crontab -l -u root | grep -i dnssec; systemctl list-timers | grep -i dns
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Scheduled cron entries or systemd timer units for dnssec-rollover or equivalent scripts indicate manual_scheduled. Absence of any scheduling artifacts alongside a KASP-managed BIND confirms automated. No entries and no KASP indicates not_configured.

option_description: Captures the end-to-end DNSSEC validation result as seen by a validating resolver traversing the full trust chain from root through TLD to the authoritative zone, classified as secure (chain validates), insecure (no signatures), bogus (signatures present but invalid), or unknown (indeterminate).
security_impact: Directly referenced in the chain_of_trust_coverage Rego rule, where dnssec_validation_chain_status == 'secure' combined with dnssec_enabled_at_zone and ds_record_published_at_parent satisfies the countermeasure. A 'bogus' status is the most dangerous outcome, as validating resolvers will SERVFAIL for all queries to the domain, causing complete DNS outage. 'Insecure' means no DNSSEC protection is in place. Only 'secure' confirms the cryptographic chain is intact end-to-end.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the domain using a DNSSEC-validating resolver with the AD (Authenticated Data) flag check. The AD flag in the response header confirms the resolver validated the full chain successfully.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response header showing 'flags: qr rd ra ad;' with an RRSIG record in the ANSWER section indicates 'secure'. Missing AD flag with no RRSIG indicates 'insecure'. SERVFAIL response indicates 'bogus'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the drill utility with DNSSEC trace mode to walk the full chain from root to zone and identify where the chain breaks if validation fails.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing successful verification at each delegation level ending with 'example.com is secure' indicates 'secure' status. Output showing 'No trusted keys found' or 'Bogus' at any level identifies the break point.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Verisign DNSSEC Debugger online tool or DNSViz to perform a visual chain-of-trust analysis that maps every delegation from root to the target zone and highlights failures.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Navigate to https://dnsviz.net/ or https://dnssec-debugger.verisignlabs.com/ and enter the target domain name to initiate a full chain analysis.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DNSViz renders a green chain diagram for 'secure', grey for 'insecure', and red broken links for 'bogus'. The debugger shows pass/fail at each delegation level.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use delv (DNS lookup and validation utility bundled with BIND) to perform local DNSSEC validation with verbose trust chain output, bypassing resolver caches.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines containing '; fully validated' and 'validation OK' indicate 'secure'. Lines containing '; unsigned answer' indicate 'insecure'. Lines containing 'DNSSEC error' or 'failed to verify' indicate 'bogus'.
